virals.hook:
Doesn't look good, my friends....

Exclusive:  Iran Doubles Down on Its Nuclear Ambitions
The Wall Street Journal 

Perceiving America as weakened, Tehran shifts from ‘no war, no peace’ to ‘maximum deterrence.’

The U.S. has seen only one major stalemated foreign conflict, in Korea. The ugly reverberations from losing against Iran today would easily be as large as what Washington would have confronted in East Asia had the communists conquered the peninsula.

If America is defeated, the Islamic Republic would control the Persian Gulf. It would have the power to enforce tolls and intrude deeply into the Arab Gulf countries’ economies and politics. Not one of these kingdoms or emirates is a strong state. And China and Russia have already seen America flustered, fearful and retrenching, unable to build sufficient interceptors to handle a Third World country. An Iranian victory would confirm for them that Washington is too politically divided and impatient to defend what once was a bipartisan strategic priority.

After rebuffing Washington and Jerusalem, Tehran appears to have come away from this war with renewed determination to acquire nuclear weapons. If Iran realizes these ambitions, America might as well close the book on its post-World War II nonproliferation mission.

A new Iranian narrative is developing: The late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei ruled for too long. An aging revolutionary, he remained antagonistic toward America but had too much respect for its power. His doctrine of “no war, no peace” meant that he would build up the atomic program but not assemble a weapon—at least not soon enough.

After Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, Khamenei didn’t meet the moment. Younger militants, mostly from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, warned him that caution could prove Iran’s undoing. When an Israeli strike in February killed the 86-year-old cleric, they concluded that being a threshold state offers insufficient protection.

Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his father, has a scant public record. He hasn’t been seen in public since the February attack, which reportedly left him badly wounded. But pronouncements issued under his name have ushered in momentous changes in Iran’s strategic outlook. President Masoud Pezeshkian announced this month: “The supreme leader ordered us to end the no war, no peace situation.” In another statement, Mojtaba Khamenei declared that given all the hostilities it was time for “maximum deterrence.”

The young Mr. Khamenei’s statements may be laced with ambiguity, but the chorus advocating the bomb isn’t. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary to Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, observed: “If a country possesses a nuclear weapon, it can be cheaper and more effective than having hundreds of F-35s and spending enormous amounts of money on other military capabilities.” The theme of deterrence was pressed by Iran’s parliamentarians. Ali Bagherzadeh claimed that “peace is achieved through strength, and the time has come to change the nuclear doctrine.” His colleague Ebrahim Rezaei similarly noted: “According to the enemy’s own admission, if we had gone nuclear . . . we would not have been attacked, and they would have dealt with us differently.”

The Assembly of Experts, which oversees the office of the supreme leader, has called for “examining the issue of withdrawing from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, reviewing the country’s defense doctrine, and creating the necessary deterrence.” It says these steps have “become an inevitable necessity and . . . a public and national demand.”

Ali Khamenei had worried that a direct confrontation with the U.S. could threaten the theocracy. Those fears conditioned his nuclear posture. His minions who survived the February attack are more confident in the regime’s resilience and are willing to cross lines that he didn’t. They have obstructed the Persian Gulf. They have paid little attention to the sensibilities of their Chinese ally, which depends on Middle Eastern oil. And they have abandoned the message discipline that Ali Khamenei imposed: They openly acclaim the virtues of nuclear arms.

Amid the debris of the U.S. midterms, the Iranian regime senses opportunities. The American people are against the Iran war. Most Democrats oppose it. And President Trump has essentially given up on it, ceasing major military operations and relying on economic coercion, which has seriously worried but so far hasn’t incapacitated Tehran. If the new Democratic Congress starves the U.S. Navy of cash for its Iran blockade and ship escorts through the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran would triumph quickly.

According to the Javan newspaper, an IRGC mouthpiece, “it is natural that America will be busy with its own domestic challenges in the next two years, and this is an opportunity for the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

Yet physics, not politics, will determine the pace of the Islamic Republic’s nuclear program. The atomic infrastructure built up over decades has been badly damaged. It will take a long time to rehabilitate. Still, a nation with a decent scientific bench and an elite united behind an atomic cause can overcome these obstacles, if unchecked by America. Tehran has always known that Washington, not Jerusalem, is the decisive enemy of its nuclear aspirations.

Ali Khamenei tried to project power by seeding the region with proxies. He and his minions regarded terrorism as both statecraft and soulcraft. His successors, who survived a massive domestic insurrection last winter as well as foreigners’ missiles and bombs, know now that proxies are no substitute for nuclear weapons. In the new Middle East, everyone’s calculations have become existential.

outsiders.hook:
Doesn't look good, my friends....

Exclusive:  Iran Doubles Down on Its Nuclear Ambitions
The Wall Street Journal 

Perceiving America as weakened, Tehran shifts from ‘no war, no peace’ to ‘maximum deterrence.’

The U.S. has seen only one major stalemated foreign conflict, in Korea. The ugly reverberations from losing against Iran today would easily be as large as what Washington would have confronted in East Asia had the communists conquered the peninsula.

If America is defeated, the Islamic Republic would control the Persian Gulf. It would have the power to enforce tolls and intrude deeply into the Arab Gulf countries’ economies and politics. Not one of these kingdoms or emirates is a strong state. And China and Russia have already seen America flustered, fearful and retrenching, unable to build sufficient interceptors to handle a Third World country. An Iranian victory would confirm for them that Washington is too politically divided and impatient to defend what once was a bipartisan strategic priority.

After rebuffing Washington and Jerusalem, Tehran appears to have come away from this war with renewed determination to acquire nuclear weapons. If Iran realizes these ambitions, America might as well close the book on its post-World War II nonproliferation mission.

A new Iranian narrative is developing: The late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei ruled for too long. An aging revolutionary, he remained antagonistic toward America but had too much respect for its power. His doctrine of “no war, no peace” meant that he would build up the atomic program but not assemble a weapon—at least not soon enough.

After Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, Khamenei didn’t meet the moment. Younger militants, mostly from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, warned him that caution could prove Iran’s undoing. When an Israeli strike in February killed the 86-year-old cleric, they concluded that being a threshold state offers insufficient protection.

Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his father, has a scant public record. He hasn’t been seen in public since the February attack, which reportedly left him badly wounded. But pronouncements issued under his name have ushered in momentous changes in Iran’s strategic outlook. President Masoud Pezeshkian announced this month: “The supreme leader ordered us to end the no war, no peace situation.” In another statement, Mojtaba Khamenei declared that given all the hostilities it was time for “maximum deterrence.”

The young Mr. Khamenei’s statements may be laced with ambiguity, but the chorus advocating the bomb isn’t. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary to Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, observed: “If a country possesses a nuclear weapon, it can be cheaper and more effective than having hundreds of F-35s and spending enormous amounts of money on other military capabilities.” The theme of deterrence was pressed by Iran’s parliamentarians. Ali Bagherzadeh claimed that “peace is achieved through strength, and the time has come to change the nuclear doctrine.” His colleague Ebrahim Rezaei similarly noted: “According to the enemy’s own admission, if we had gone nuclear . . . we would not have been attacked, and they would have dealt with us differently.”

The Assembly of Experts, which oversees the office of the supreme leader, has called for “examining the issue of withdrawing from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, reviewing the country’s defense doctrine, and creating the necessary deterrence.” It says these steps have “become an inevitable necessity and . . . a public and national demand.”

Ali Khamenei had worried that a direct confrontation with the U.S. could threaten the theocracy. Those fears conditioned his nuclear posture. His minions who survived the February attack are more confident in the regime’s resilience and are willing to cross lines that he didn’t. They have obstructed the Persian Gulf. They have paid little attention to the sensibilities of their Chinese ally, which depends on Middle Eastern oil. And they have abandoned the message discipline that Ali Khamenei imposed: They openly acclaim the virtues of nuclear arms.

Amid the debris of the U.S. midterms, the Iranian regime senses opportunities. The American people are against the Iran war. Most Democrats oppose it. And President Trump has essentially given up on it, ceasing major military operations and relying on economic coercion, which has seriously worried but so far hasn’t incapacitated Tehran. If the new Democratic Congress starves the U.S. Navy of cash for its Iran blockade and ship escorts through the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran would triumph quickly.

According to the Javan newspaper, an IRGC mouthpiece, “it is natural that America will be busy with its own domestic challenges in the next two years, and this is an opportunity for the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

Yet physics, not politics, will determine the pace of the Islamic Republic’s nuclear program. The atomic infrastructure built up over decades has been badly damaged. It will take a long time to rehabilitate. Still, a nation with a decent scientific bench and an elite united behind an atomic cause can overcome these obstacles, if unchecked by America. Tehran has always known that Washington, not Jerusalem, is the decisive enemy of its nuclear aspirations.

Ali Khamenei tried to project power by seeding the region with proxies. He and his minions regarded terrorism as both statecraft and soulcraft. His successors, who survived a massive domestic insurrection last winter as well as foreigners’ missiles and bombs, know now that proxies are no substitute for nuclear weapons. In the new Middle East, everyone’s calculations have become existential.
